# spHawkes <img src="man/figures/logo.png" align="right" height="139" alt="spHawkes logo" />

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![pkgdown](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/actions/workflows/pkgdown.yaml)
[![test-coverage](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/actions/workflows/test-coverage.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/actions/workflows/test-coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

Semi-parametric self-exciting (Hawkes) spatio-temporal point process models, fit via a stochastic-declustering EM algorithm (following Zhuang & Mateu, 2019). This package works on **any** properly projected `sf` point dataset and study-region polygon.

The package provides:

- **Data preparation** for `sf` points and a study-region polygon, with
  checks on the coordinate reference system and the study period
  (`prepare_events()`).
- **Model fitting** by the EM algorithm, with non-parametric trend, weekly,
  monthly and spatial background components and non-parametric triggering
  kernels in time and space (`fit_semihawkes()`).
- **Goodness-of-fit diagnostics**: time-transformed residuals, and residuals
  by calendar period and by area (`gof_time_transform()`,
  `gof_period_residuals()`, `gof_spatial_residuals()`).
- **Intensity maps** of the background and triggering intensity on a grid,
  as snapshots or animations (`background_trigger_grid()`,
  `plot_intensity_snapshot()`, `animate_intensity_snapshots()`).
- **Uncertainty in the branching structure**: Monte Carlo samples of which
  events are background and which are triggered (`sample_branching()`,
  `sample_branching_multi()`, `summarize_branching_samples()`).

## The model

The model describes the rate at which events occur at location $(x, y)$ and
time $t$, given the history $\mathcal{H}_t$ of events before $t$. This
conditional intensity is a background rate plus the extra rate triggered by
earlier events:

$$
\lambda(x, y, t \mid \mathcal{H}_t) = \underbrace{\mu_0\, \mu_T(t)\, \mu_m(t)\, \mu_w(t)\, \mu_b(x, y)}_{\text{background}}+\underbrace{A \int_{-\infty}^{t} \int_{W} g(t - s)\, h(x - u,\, y - v)\, N(du\, dv\, ds)}_{\text{triggering}}
$$

Here $W$ is the study region and $N$ is the counting measure of the events:
it puts a mass of 1 at the location $(x_i, y_i)$ and time $t_i$ of each
event, so the triggering term adds up $A\, g(t - t_i)\, h(x - x_i,\, y - y_i)$
over the events $i$ before $t$.

- **Background.** $\mu_0$ is a constant rate. $\mu_T(t)$, $\mu_m(t)$ and
  $\mu_w(t)$ multiply it by a long-term trend, a calendar-month effect and a
  day-of-week effect, each averaging 1, and $\mu_b(x, y)$ is a spatial surface
  that averages 1 over the study region.
- **Triggering.** Each earlier event $i$, at $(x_i, y_i)$ and time $t_i$,
  raises the rate nearby for a while. The temporal kernel $g$ describes how
  this extra rate fades with the time since the event, and the spatial kernel
  $h$ how it fades with distance from it. Both integrate to 1, so the
  **branching ratio** $A$ is the expected number of events that each event
  triggers directly.

The model is semi-parametric: the six functions $\mu_T$, $\mu_m$, $\mu_w$,
$\mu_b$, $g$ and $h$ are estimated non-parametrically, by kernel smoothing,
while $\mu_0$ and $A$ are numerical parameters. The EM algorithm alternates two
steps until the fit settles. The E-step computes, for each event $i$, the
probability that it is a background event,

$$
\varphi_i = \frac{\mu_0\, \mu_T(t_i)\, \mu_m(t_i)\, \mu_w(t_i)\, \mu_b(x_i, y_i)}{\lambda(x_i, y_i, t_i \mid \mathcal{H}_{t_i})},
$$

and, for each earlier event $j$, the probability that $j$ triggered $i$,

$$
\rho_{ij} = \frac{A\, g(t_i - t_j)\, h(x_i - x_j,\, y_i - y_j)}{\lambda(x_i, y_i, t_i \mid \mathcal{H}_{t_i})}.
$$

The M-step then re-estimates every component from the events, weighted by
these probabilities.

## What it produces

A worked example on the simulated dataset bundled with the package
(`?sim_events`): 375 events over three years on an 8 km square region, drawn
from a branching process with a known branching ratio of `A = 0.35`, three
spatial hotspots, a rising trend and elevated weekends.

In a branching process every event is one of two kinds. **Background** events
arise independently of one another, at a rate that depends only on place and
time (here the hotspots, the trend and the weekend effect). **Triggered**
events are the offspring of an earlier event, and occur near it in space and
soon after it in time (for instance, events within 300 m and 5 days). Every
event, of either kind, can trigger offspring of its own, so a single
background event can set off a chain.

The **branching ratio** $A$ is the expected number of offspring that each
event triggers directly. With $A = 0.35$, 100 events trigger about 35 more,
which trigger about 12 more in turn, and so on. These generations form a
geometric series, so each background event leads to $1/(1 - A)$ events on
average, itself included (about 1.5 here), and in the long run a fraction $A$
of all events are triggered (35% here). This needs $A$ below 1: an $A$ near 0
describes a pattern that is almost all background, and an $A$ near 1 one
dominated by contagion.

The fit below gives the triggering kernel a reach of 1 km from each event,
set through the kernel grid's `x_range` and `trigger_window_dist`. That is
also the default, but the reach should be chosen with care for every
dataset: make it a few times the distance over which one event can plausibly
trigger another (here, offspring fall a few hundred metres from their
parent). A much wider reach lets the kernel's tail absorb clustering in the
background, which inflates the estimated branching ratio; see *Choosing the
triggering reach* in `?fit_semihawkes`.

```{r fit, results = "hide"}
library(spHawkes)
library(sf)

fit <- fit_semihawkes(
  points    = sim_events,
  region    = sim_region,
  date_col  = "date",
  cell_size = 400,
  cache_dir = tempfile("spHawkes_marks_"),
  bandwidth_args = list(k = 5, min_dist = 150, min_bandwidth = 300),
  trigger_window_dist  = 1000,
  trigger_spatial_args = list(x_range = 1000),
  n_iter    = 12,
  verbose   = FALSE
)
```

`summary()` reports the study window, the estimated parameters, and how the
observed events divide between persistent background risk and contagion:

```{r summary}
summary(fit)
```

Because this dataset was simulated, its generating values are known: the
branching ratio was `A = 0.35`, and 115 of the 375 realised events (30.7%)
were triggered. That share is below 35% mainly by chance, because the number
of offspring is random; a few offspring were also discarded because they fell
outside the region or after the end of the three years. The summary above
reports the fitted counterparts: an estimated branching ratio of
`r format(round(fit$A, 2), nsmall = 2)`, and an estimated share of triggered
events of `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (1 - mean(fit$bgprobs)))`, the average
fitted probability that an event was triggered rather than background. They
need not match the generating values exactly.

This example uses a fixed budget of 12 EM iterations. In the run shown,
the algorithm reached that limit without satisfying the convergence
criterion, so these results should be treated as an illustration rather
than a converged estimate or evidence of estimator accuracy. See
`tests/testthat/test-recovery.R` for the recovery tests.

The model decomposes risk into a **background** surface, capturing stable
place-based risk, and a **triggering** kernel, capturing how each event raises
the risk of further events nearby and soon after. Those two things call for
different responses, which is the point of separating them.

```{r components, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 5), cex.main = 1.05)

# (a) the observed pattern
xy <- st_coordinates(sim_events)
plot(xy, type = "n", asp = 1, main = "(a) Observed events",
     xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "y (m)")
plot(st_geometry(sim_region), col = "grey96", border = "grey55", add = TRUE)
points(xy, pch = 16, cex = 0.45, col = adjustcolor("firebrick", 0.65))

# (b) the estimated background surface: where risk persists
bg <- fit$background$basevalue
bg[fit$background$marks == 0] <- NA
fields::image.plot(fit$background$x, fit$background$y, bg,
                   main = "(b) Background surface", xlab = "x (m)", ylab = "y (m)",
                   col = hcl.colors(64, "Blues", rev = TRUE))
plot(st_geometry(sim_region), add = TRUE, border = "grey35", lwd = 1.5)

# (c) how long a triggered effect lasts
g <- fit$temporal_trigger
keep <- g$base <= 40
plot(g$base[keep], g$basevalue[keep], type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = "#2f6b52",
     main = "(c) Triggering: time since event", xlab = "Days", ylab = "Density")
polygon(c(g$base[keep], rev(g$base[keep])),
        c(g$basevalue[keep], rep(0, sum(keep))),
        col = adjustcolor("#2f6b52", 0.18), border = NA)

# (d) how far it reaches
h <- fit$spatial_trigger
win <- abs(h$x) <= 2000
fields::image.plot(h$x[win], h$y[win], h$basevalue[win, win] * 1e6,
                   main = "(d) Triggering: distance from event",
                   xlab = "x offset (m)", ylab = "y offset (m)",
                   col = hcl.colors(64, "Greens 3", rev = TRUE),
                   legend.args = list(text = expression("per " * km^2),
                                      side = 3, line = 0.6, cex = 0.85))
par(op)
```

Panel (b) is the geography of *persistent* risk; panels (c) and (d) say how
long and how far a single event's influence extends.

Convergence over the EM iterations is shown below. The EM was capped at 12
iterations here for brevity, so the curves have not fully levelled off; by
default, `fit_semihawkes()` runs up to 50 iterations and stops earlier once
the log-likelihood settles.

```{r history, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 9, echo = FALSE}
plot(fit, which = "history")
```

## Installation

Install the released state of `main` directly from GitHub:

``` r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes")
```

`install_github()` does not build the vignettes by default. To install them
as well, ask for them. This needs the suggested packages, hence
`dependencies = TRUE`, and takes several minutes, because the vignettes fit
models:

``` r
remotes::install_github("HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes",
                        build_vignettes = TRUE, dependencies = TRUE)
```

To work on the package itself, clone it and load it in place:

``` r
# git clone https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes.git
devtools::load_all(".")   # load without installing
devtools::install(".")    # or install from the local source
```

Dependencies (`fields`, `foreach`, `ggplot2`, `patchwork`, `rlang`, `scales`, `sf`, `spatstat.geom`, `spatstat.random`, `units`) are all on CRAN, and `parallel` ships with R. Note that, when built from source, `sf` needs the system GDAL, GEOS and PROJ libraries and `units` needs udunits2; see the [`sf` installation notes](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/#installing) if the install fails while compiling them.

## Usage: full pipeline

``` r
library(spHawkes)
library(sf)

# `crime_points`: an sf POINT layer with a date column, any CRS.
# `city`: an sf POLYGON/MULTIPOLYGON study-region boundary.

fit <- fit_semihawkes(
  points     = crime_points,
  region     = city,
  date_col   = "fecha_infraccion",
  cell_size  = 150,                   # spatial background grid cell size (required)
  cache_dir  = "cache/spatial_marks", # trigger_spatial_marks() cache (required)
  start_date = "2014-01-01",          # optional; defaults to earliest event date
  end_date   = "2025-01-01",          # optional; defaults to latest event date + 1
  crs        = 32717,                 # optional; defaults to the region's CRS
  bandwidth_args = list(k = 5, min_dist = 150),
  n_iter = 50,
  tol    = 0.001,
  tol_A  = 0.001,
  nprocs = 1                          # set > 1 for parallel trigger evaluation
)

print(fit)
fit$history                 # per-iteration mu, A, llik, lambda_at_all
plot(fit, which = "history")
plot(fit, which = "background")
plot(fit, which = "trigger_spatial")
```

## Usage: individual building blocks

The pipeline above is built from smaller, independently usable functions -- useful when you want to inspect or debug a single stage without running the full EM loop:

``` r
ev <- prepare_events(
  points     = crime_points,
  region     = city,
  date_col   = "fecha_infraccion",
  start_date = "2014-01-01",
  end_date   = "2025-01-01",
  crs        = 32717
)
print(ev)   # counts kept/dropped, study period, CRS
summary(ev)

ev <- add_adaptive_bandwidth(ev, k = 5, min_dist = 150, min_bandwidth = 250)
ev <- add_bg_integral(ev, n_mc = 3000)

trend   <- temporal_base_trend(ev)
weekly  <- temporal_base_weekly(ev)
monthly <- temporal_base_monthly(ev)
background <- background_spatial(ev, cell_size = 150)

temporal_trigger <- trigger_temporal_init()
spatial_trigger  <- trigger_spatial_init()

trig <- trigger_evaluate(ev, background, temporal_trigger, spatial_trigger)
```

`prepare_events()` enforces the checks that matter for reproducing this on a new dataset:

-   `points` must be an `sf` object with `POINT` geometry.

-   `region` must be an `sf`/`sfc` object with `POLYGON`/`MULTIPOLYGON` geometry.

-   Both must have a CRS set, and the working CRS -- the region's, or an explicit `crs=` argument -- must be **projected** (metres, not degrees): kernel bandwidths and distances throughout the package are in linear units. A geographic (lon/lat) working CRS raises an informative error telling you to `sf::st_transform()` first.

-   `points` is reprojected to the working CRS automatically, so it can be supplied in any CRS, including lon/lat.

-   Events outside `region` or outside `[start_date, end_date)` are dropped, and the returned object reports exactly how many/why, so a new dataset's filtering behaviour is easy to sanity-check.

## Learn more

The [package website](https://henriquescadbylab.github.io/spHawkes/) has the full function reference and four
articles:

-   [Getting started with spHawkes](https://henriquescadbylab.github.io/spHawkes/articles/getting-started.html): the whole workflow on the simulated data, from preparing events and fitting the model to checking convergence, reading the fitted components and assessing goodness of fit.

-   [Separating background risk from contagion](https://henriquescadbylab.github.io/spHawkes/articles/background-and-triggering.html): why the two call for different responses, and how to map where each one dominates.

-   [Uncertainty quantification for the branching structure](https://henriquescadbylab.github.io/spHawkes/articles/branching-structure-uq.html): sampling which events are background and which are triggered, so that summaries of the two come with confidence bands instead of a single estimate.

-   [Modelling drug-related deaths in Milwaukee County](https://henriquescadbylab.github.io/spHawkes/articles/milwaukee-drug-deaths.html): a worked example on real data, with exploratory plots, diagnostics, intensity maps and an animation.

The articles are also the package's vignettes: `browseVignettes("spHawkes")`
lists them if you installed them (see Installation above).

Beyond fitting a model, the package can:

-   **Explore the data first**: `plot_event_summary()` and `inspect_spatial_grid()`.

-   **Check a fit**: `gof_time_transform()`, `gof_spatial_residuals()` and `gof_period_residuals()`, each with a `plot()` method.

-   **Map the fitted intensity**: `background_trigger_grid()`, `plot_intensity_snapshot()`, `animate_intensity_snapshots()` and `integrate_intensity_period()`.

-   **Quantify uncertainty in the branching structure**: `sample_branching_multi()` and `summarize_branching_samples()`.

Three example datasets are bundled, each with its study region:

-   `sim_events` and `sim_region`: 375 simulated events over three years on an 8 km square region, with known generating values.

-   `crimes` and `crimes_region`: about 2,300 events simulated from a model fitted to open homicide data from Guayaquil, Ecuador.

-   `milwaukee` and `milwaukee_county`: more than 3,000 drug-related deaths recorded in Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, from 2020 onwards (real data).

Their help pages (`?sim_events`, `?crimes`, `?milwaukee`) describe how each
was built and where it comes from.

The method follows [Zhuang and Mateu (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssa.12429).
To cite the package, see `citation("spHawkes")`.

spHawkes began as a port of the R code that accompanies
[D'Angelo et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1177/1471082X221094146), which
implements this method. It has since been substantially rewritten: several
errors in that code have been fixed, and its slowest computations have been
rewritten to run much faster. The model and the estimation method are the
same.

## Development

``` r
devtools::document()   # regenerate NAMESPACE/man/ from roxygen comments
devtools::test()       # run the testthat suite
devtools::check()      # full R CMD check
pkgdown::build_site()  # build the documentation site into docs/ (not committed)
```

`devtools::document()` is pinned to the roxygen2 version recorded in
`DESCRIPTION`'s `RoxygenNote`. If you regenerate the docs with a different
version, every file in `man/` will churn, so it is worth checking that field
before running it.

### Continuous integration

Three workflows run on every push to `main` and on every pull request. All
three can also be started by hand from the repository's **Actions** tab
(`Run workflow`), and each is capped with a timeout so a stalled job cannot
run away.

| Workflow | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`R-CMD-check`](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/blob/main/.github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml) | `R CMD check --as-cran` on Linux (current R and the previous release), macOS and Windows. This is the one that has to be green. |
| [`pkgdown`](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/blob/main/.github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml) | Builds the documentation site. On a pull request it builds but does not publish, so a broken roxygen link or a failing example is caught before it reaches the site. |
| [`test-coverage`](https://github.com/HenriquesCadbyLab/spHawkes/blob/main/.github/workflows/test-coverage.yaml) | Runs the suite under `covr` and uploads a `coverage-report` artifact, downloadable from the run's summary page. |

Each workflow installs GDAL, GEOS, PROJ and udunits before setting up R.
That step is only a fallback -- `setup-r-dependencies` already resolves system
requirements through `pak`, and `use-public-rspm` supplies Linux binaries -- so
it is bounded by a timeout and marked `continue-on-error`. A slow package
mirror will not wedge or fail a run.

### Publishing the documentation site

The `pkgdown` workflow writes the built site to a `gh-pages` branch, which it
creates on its first successful run on `main`. Serving it needs one setting,
which only a repository **admin** can change:

> **Settings -> Pages -> Build and deployment**
> Source: `Deploy from a branch`, Branch: `gh-pages`, Folder: `/ (root)`

Once set, the site is published at <https://henriquescadbylab.github.io/spHawkes/>,
matching the `url:` field in `_pkgdown.yml`. Until then the workflow still runs
and still catches documentation errors -- the site simply is not served.
